title: Working with Files
summary: Read, write and append text files with node:fs/promises, build paths that work from any folder, handle missing files, list directories and keep data in a JSON file.
introduction: Servers read configuration, write logs, accept uploads and cache results; scripts rename, convert and clean up files. All of that goes through the `node:fs` module. This lesson uses its promise-based API, which fits naturally with `async`/`await`, and covers the handful of operations you need most, plus the two mistakes nearly everyone makes once: forgetting the text encoding and assuming a relative path is relative to the script.
learningObjectives: Read, write and append files asynchronously with node:fs/promises
Build reliable paths with node:path and import.meta.dirname
Handle missing files, create folders, list directory contents and store JSON data

blocks.text: `node:fs/promises` exports functions that return promises. `writeFile` creates or replaces a file, `appendFile` adds to the end, and `readFile` returns the contents. Passing `'utf8'` as the encoding turns the raw bytes into a string:

blocks.title: todo.js
Forgetting the encoding
blocks.text: Without `'utf8'`, `readFile` resolves with a **Buffer**, Node's type for raw bytes, and `console.log` prints `<Buffer 42 75 79 20 6d 69 6c 6b 0a 43 61 6c 6c 20 41 64 61 0a>` instead of your text. Buffers are right for images and archives; for anything you want to read as text, pass the encoding or call `.toString()`.
Paths that work from any folder

A relative path such as `'todo.txt'` is resolved against the **current working directory**: the folder your terminal was in when you ran `node`, not the folder that contains the script. Running `node src/todo.js` from the project root therefore creates `todo.txt` in the root, and running the same script from another folder creates it somewhere else. For files that belong to the program, anchor the path to the module's own folder with `import.meta.dirname` and join the pieces with `node:path`, which also uses the right separator on Windows:

blocks.title: where.js

blocks.text: `resolve` turns a relative path into an absolute one using the working directory, which is exactly what `readFile('todo.txt')` does internally; printing it is a quick way to see where a file will really end up.

File operations fail for everyday reasons: the file is not there yet, the folder is read-only, a disk is full. The rejected promise carries an error whose `code` property names the cause; `ENOENT` means *no such file or directory*. Check the code so that you handle the expected case and let anything unexpected crash loudly:

blocks.text: `mkdir` with `recursive: true` creates a whole chain of folders and does not complain if they already exist. `readdir` lists a folder; with `withFileTypes: true` each entry knows whether it is a file or a directory, which saves a `stat` call per entry. The operating system decides the order of the listing, so sort it when the order matters:

blocks.title: reports.js

blocks.text: `stat` returns size, timestamps (`mtime` is the last modification) and the same `isFile()`/`isDirectory()` checks. To delete, use `rm(path)` for a file and `rm(path, { recursive: true, force: true })` for a folder tree; `force` suppresses the error when the target does not exist.

Before reaching for a database, many small tools keep their data in a JSON file. The pattern is always the same: read and parse (treating a missing file as empty), change the array in memory, then serialise and write the whole file back. `JSON.stringify(notes, null, 2)` indents the output so that the file stays readable in an editor:

blocks.title: notes.js

blocks.code:
node notes.js "Read about streams"
node notes.js "Try node:sqlite"

blocks.title: Terminal
blocks.content:
Saved 1 note(s) to notes.json
Saved 2 note(s) to notes.json

blocks.text: Every function above has a synchronous twin in `node:fs`: `readFileSync`, `writeFileSync`, `mkdirSync`, `existsSync` and so on. They block the whole process until the disk answers, which is harmless in a short script or while a server is starting up (loading a config file before `listen`), and harmful inside a request handler, where one slow read freezes every other request. Rule of thumb: synchronous at startup, asynchronous once the program is serving.

blocks.title: Large files
blocks.text: `readFile` loads the entire file into memory. For logs, exports and uploads that may be gigabytes, read them piece by piece with streams; the [next lesson](/tutorials/nodejs/events-streams) shows how.

questions.question: You run `node tools/export.js` from the project root. Where does `writeFile('out.csv', data)` create the file?
questions.explanation: Relative paths resolve against the current working directory (the folder the terminal was in), not against the script's folder. Use import.meta.dirname to anchor paths to the script.
options: It throws because the path is relative

questions.question: `mkdir('a/b/c', { recursive: true })` throws if the folder `a` already exists.
questions.explanation: With recursive: true, mkdir creates whichever parts of the chain are missing and succeeds silently when the folders already exist.
